UNCLAIMED FINAL WAGES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS UNCLAIMED FINAL WAGES INFORMATION SHEET
Re: Unclaimed Final Wages — Jordan Lee

This information sheet describes California's Unclaimed Property Law (Code of Civil Procedure § 1500 et seq.) as it applies to final wages that Acme, Inc. owes to Jordan Lee but has been unable to deliver because Jordan Lee cannot be located or has not claimed them. Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. ended on September 30, 2026. It is a companion to, and does not repeat, this document set's separate Final Paycheck Delivery Method and Location information sheet, which addresses how and where a final paycheck must be delivered when the employer knows where to send it; this document instead addresses what the statute says happens when that delivery cannot be completed because the wages go unclaimed. It states facts about what the statute requires of a holder of unpaid wages; it does not determine that these particular wages are, or are not, subject to escheat, and it does not tell Acme, Inc. what to do about this specific unpaid amount.

THE ONE-YEAR DORMANCY PERIOD FOR UNCLAIMED WAGES
California's Unclaimed Property Law sets a general three-year dormancy period for most kinds of unclaimed personal property held in the ordinary course of a holder's business, but wages and salaries are carved out and given a shorter, specific period of their own: any wages or salaries that have remained unclaimed by the owner for more than one year after they become payable escheat to the state. This one-year wage rule sits within the same statutory section that lists other categories of property (chiefly bank and financial-organization deposits and accounts) escheating on their own separate terms, and it applies to wages or salaries held or owing by a "business association" -- a term the statute defines broadly to include private corporations, business trusts, partnerships, and other business associations of two or more people, whether or not organized for profit. Unpaid wages currently identified for Jordan Lee as of September 30, 2026 total $3,200.00, according to Acme, Inc.'s records.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any wages or salaries that have remained unclaimed by the owner for more than one year after the wages or salaries become payable."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1513, subd. (a)(7), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1513, subd. (a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1513.)
  "Subject to Sections 1510 and 1511, the following property held or owing by a business association escheats to this state:"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1513, subd. (a), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1513, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1513.)
  "“Business association” means any private corporation, joint stock company, business trust, partnership, or any association for business purposes of two or more individuals, whether or not for profit, including, but not by way of limitation, a banking organization, financial organization, life insurance corporation, and utility."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1501, subd. (c), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1501, subd. (c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that wages are treated as their own category of unclaimed property with a one-year dormancy period distinct from the three-year general rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that these specific wages have, in fact, gone unclaimed for the necessary period. The one-year wage provision and the statutory definition of "business association" both come from the Unclaimed Property Law but are, respectively, a single statutory paragraph (§ 1513, subd. (a)(7)) and a single statutory subdivision of a different, definitional section (§ 1501, subd. (c)); the two citations below are not independent of one another within each grouping, though the definitional citation is a genuinely separate section from the dormancy-period citation. This document does not address how an employer's holder status might differ for a sole proprietor or other holder that does not meet the statutory definition of "business association," which this research did not investigate further.

THE PRE-REPORT NOTICE REQUIREMENT AND ITS DOLLAR THRESHOLD
Before unclaimed property becomes reportable to the State Controller, the Unclaimed Property Law requires a holder that has an apparent owner's address on file -- and whose records do not show that address to be inaccurate -- to make reasonable efforts to notify the owner by mail (or electronically, if the owner has consented to electronic notice) that the property will escheat to the state, but only where the property is valued at fifty dollars ($50) or more. That notice must be mailed not less than six nor more than twelve months before the property becomes reportable to the Controller, and the statute prescribes specific required content for it, including a heading stating that California law requires notification that the property may be transferred to the state.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (a) of Section 1513.5, subdivision (b) of Section 1514, subdivision (d) of Section 1516, and subdivisions (b) and (c) of Section 1516.5, if the holder has in its records an address for the apparent owner of property valued at fifty dollars ($50) or more, which the holder’s records do not disclose to be inaccurate, the holder shall make reasonable efforts to notify the owner by mail or, if the owner has consented to electronic notice, electronically, that the owner’s property will escheat to the state pursuant to this chapter. The notice shall be mailed not less than 6 nor more than 12 months before the time when the owner’s property held by the business becomes reportable to the Controller in accordance with this chapter."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1520, subd. (b), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1520, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1520.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a $50 pre-report notice threshold and a 6-to-12-month notice window within the Unclaimed Property Law -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount. The quoted notice requirement appears in Code of Civil Procedure § 1520, subdivision (b), a section whose subdivision (a) sets the general three-year dormancy period and, by its own terms, excludes wage property covered by § 1513 from that three-year rule. Subdivision (b)'s notice duty is worded more broadly, applying to property that "will escheat to the state pursuant to this chapter" (not just property escheating under subdivision (a) of the same section), and it lists specific exceptions for property already covered by other sections' own notice rules -- Section 1513.5 (bank and financial-organization deposits), Section 1514, Section 1516, and Section 1516.5 -- without listing wages under Section 1513 among those exceptions. This document reads that structure as meaning the general $50/6-to-12-month notice duty in § 1520(b) is the one that applies to unclaimed wages under § 1513(a)(7), since no other section in this chapter was located that sets out a separate, wage-specific pre-report notice rule. That reading is not stated in so many words anywhere in the statutory text, so it is disclosed here as an inference from the section's structure and cross-references rather than as an explicit statutory statement naming wages.

THE ANNUAL REPORT TO THE STATE CONTROLLER
The Unclaimed Property Law requires every person holding property that has escheated to the state under this chapter -- a category that includes unclaimed wages -- to report that property to the State Controller. For most holders, that report must be filed before November 1 of each year, covering property status as of the preceding June 30 (or the holder's fiscal year end).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every person holding funds or other property escheated to this state under this chapter shall report to the Controller as provided in this section."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1530, subd. (a), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1530, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1530.)
  "The report shall be filed before November 1 of each year as of June 30 or fiscal yearend next preceding"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1530, subd. (d), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1530, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1530.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the general reporting duty and its annual November 1 filing deadline -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that November 1 is the deadline for every category of holder (the statute sets an earlier May 1 deadline for life insurance corporations and certain demutualization proceeds, which this document does not address because it is outside the wage scenario this document covers). Both citations below come from the same statutory section (§ 1530, subds. (a) and (d)) and are not independent of one another.

THE DEADLINE FOR DELIVERING UNCLAIMED WAGES TO THE CONTROLLER
Filing the annual report is not, by itself, the end of the process: the Unclaimed Property Law separately requires every person who filed that report to actually pay or deliver the escheated property to the Controller within a specific window measured from the report's filing deadline -- no sooner than seven months, and no later than seven months and fifteen days, after the final date for filing the report. The Controller may postpone this payment-or-delivery date, and the report deadline, on the Controller's own motion or on written request from the holder.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every person filing a report as provided by Section 1530 shall, no sooner than seven months and no later than seven months and 15 days after the final date for filing the report, pay or deliver to the Controller all escheated property specified in the report."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1532, subd. (a), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1532, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1532.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific remittance window that follows the annual report -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim about whether a postponement has been sought or granted in any specific case. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 1532, subd. (a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

DISCHARGE OF THE HOLDER'S LIABILITY, AND HOW A FORMER EMPLOYEE LATER CLAIMS THE WAGES
Once escheated property is paid or delivered to the Controller, the state assumes custody of it, and a holder who made that payment or delivery -- having made reasonable efforts to notify the owner in substantial compliance with the statute's notice provisions, where the holder had an address on file that its records did not show to be inaccurate -- is relieved of all liability, to the extent of the value of the property delivered, for any claim on that property that then exists or that might later arise. A former employee (or, after their death, their heirs or estate representative) can later recover wages that were escheated to the state by filing a verified claim with the Controller on a Controller-prescribed form; the Controller must consider the claim, and may hold a hearing and take evidence, within 180 days of filing, but no interest is payable on a claim paid under this chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Upon the payment or delivery of escheated property to the Controller, the state shall assume custody and shall be responsible for the safekeeping of the property. Any person who pays or delivers escheated property to the Controller under this chapter and who, prior to escheat, if the person’s records contain an address for the apparent owner that the holder’s records do not disclose to be inaccurate, has made reasonable efforts to notify the owner by mail or, if the owner has consented to electronic notice, electronically, in substantial compliance with Sections 1513.5, 1514, 1516, and 1520, that the owner’s property, deposit, account, shares, or other interest will escheat to the state, is relieved of all liability to the extent of the value of the property so paid or delivered for any claim that then exists or that thereafter may arise or be made in respect to the property."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1560, subd. (a), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1560, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1560.)
  "Any person, excluding another state, who claims to have been the owner, as defined in subdivision (d), of property paid or delivered to the Controller under this chapter may file a claim to the property or to the net proceeds from its sale."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1540, subds. (a)-(c), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1540, subds. (a)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1540.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the discharge-from-liability rule and the claims process available afterward -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that any specific delivery to the Controller has occurred here or that this discharge rule has already been triggered for these wages. The discharge provision (§ 1560, subd. (a)) conditions relief from liability on notice given "in substantial compliance with Sections 1513.5, 1514, 1516, and 1520" -- a list that does not name Section 1513 (the wage provision) by number. Read together with the pre-report notice clause elsewhere in this document, which explains why this document treats Section 1520's general notice duty as the one that applies to wages, this document treats that Section 1520 reference in the discharge provision as covering wage holders as well; that reading is an inference from cross-referenced statutory structure, not an explicit statement in the discharge provision itself naming wages. The two citations below come from two separate, independently numbered sections (§§ 1560 and 1540) and are independent sources of each other.

INTEREST FOR FAILURE TO REPORT, PAY, OR DELIVER UNCLAIMED PROPERTY ON TIME
The Unclaimed Property Law attaches a specific consequence to a holder's failure to meet its reporting or remittance deadlines: unless the failure is due to reasonable cause, a holder who fails to report, pay, or deliver unclaimed property within the time the statute prescribes must pay the Controller interest at the rate of 12 percent per year on that property (or its value), running from the date the property should have been reported, paid, or delivered. This interest is owed to the Controller, not to the former employee, and is separate from any damages, penalties, or fines the holder may face under other laws.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In addition to any damages, penalties, or fines for which a person may be liable under other provisions of law, any person who fails to report, pay, or deliver unclaimed property within the time prescribed by this chapter, unless that failure is due to reasonable cause, shall pay to the Controller interest at the rate of 12 percent per annum on that property or value thereof from the date the property should have been reported, paid, or delivered."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1577, subd. (a), Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1577, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1577.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific interest rate and trigger for late reporting or remittance -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that any specific deadline in this case has, in fact, been missed. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 1577, subd. (a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point. The same section caps interest at $10,000 in one narrow circumstance (a report that is filed and paid on time but not in substantial compliance with the reporting-content requirements) and allows the Controller to waive the interest for reasonable cause or full participation in a voluntary compliance program; this document does not address those provisions in further detail.

UNCLAIMED FINAL WAGES — RECORDKEEPING WORKSHEET
This worksheet records Acme, Inc.'s files concerning the unclaimed final wages described in this document, for Acme, Inc.'s own recordkeeping.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Employment end date: September 30, 2026
Amount currently identified as unpaid and unclaimed: $3,200.00
Last known address on file for Jordan Lee: 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105

Prepared by (name and title): _______________
Date prepared: _______________

This worksheet is a record of facts as Acme, Inc. currently understands them. It does not itself determine that these wages are subject to escheat under California's Unclaimed Property Law, and it does not state a reporting or remittance deadline for this specific amount.
